summary: FireWatch Cambodia is a fire-monitoring and prediction web application developed to address NASA's challenge of harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS hotspot data. Using NASA's satellite observations from the Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), we collect, process, and harmonize fire hotspot records to support more consistent fire monitoring across Cambodia. The platform visualizes historical fire activity, identifies seasonal patterns, and analyzes unusual hotspot activity. Building on this harmonized dataset, we developed and deployed a machine learning model to predict areas with potentially higher future fire risk. The results are presented through an interactive map, allowing users to explore historical hotspots and potential future risk areas. By going beyond the visualization of past fire events, FireWatch Cambodia demonstrates how combining NASA satellite data, data science, and machine learning can support forward-looking fire monitoring. This project aims to improve awareness of potential fire-risk areas, support environmental monitoring, and provide useful information for communities, researchers, and decision-makers in Cambodia.
details:
FireWatch Cambodia

1. Project Overview

FireWatch Cambodia is a satellite-based fire monitoring and prediction platform developed in response to NASA's challenge, Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots. The project aims to improve the understanding of fire activity across Cambodia by combining observations from two NASA satellite instruments: the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) and the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS).

These satellite systems provide valuable active fire observations, but their differences in spatial resolution and detection characteristics make direct comparison challenging. FireWatch Cambodia addresses this challenge by collecting, processing, and harmonizing their hotspot datasets into a more consistent data structure.

Beyond historical fire visualization, our project incorporates data science and machine learning to analyze historical fire activity and predict areas with potentially higher future fire risk. The results are presented through an interactive web application, allowing users to explore historical hotspots, understand fire patterns, and view predicted risk areas.

Our goal is to demonstrate how harmonized NASA satellite observations and machine learning can support more informed environmental monitoring and fire-risk assessment in Cambodia.

2. How It Works – Key Technical Innovations

2.1. Satellite Data Collection

The project uses active fire and hotspot observations from NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS). We collect data from two satellite instruments:

  • MODIS: Provides active fire observations with approximately 1 km spatial resolution.
  • VIIRS: Provides active fire observations with approximately 375 m spatial resolution for its standard 375 m active fire product.

The datasets contain information such as geographic coordinates, acquisition dates and times, confidence levels, and other fire-related attributes.

2.2. Data Cleaning and Harmonization

Since MODIS and VIIRS have different spatial resolutions and detection characteristics, their observations cannot simply be treated as identical measurements.

Our data processing workflow includes:

  • Cleaning and standardizing the collected datasets.
  • Handling missing values and inconsistent data formats.
  • Standardizing relevant attributes and geographic information.
  • Comparing observations from MODIS and VIIRS.
  • Combining processed records into a structured master dataset.

This process provides a foundation for analyzing observations from both satellite systems together while retaining their original data sources.

2.3. Historical Fire Pattern Analysis

After harmonization, we analyze historical hotspot observations to understand fire activity across Cambodia.

The analysis focuses on:

  • Geographic distribution of fire hotspots.
  • Monthly and seasonal fire activity.
  • Changes in hotspot frequency over time.
  • Differences and similarities between MODIS and VIIRS observations.
  • Unusual increases in hotspot activity.

These analyses help identify recurring patterns and areas that may require closer monitoring. By examining historical observations across different locations and time periods, users can better understand how fire activity changes over time.

2.4. Machine Learning-Based Fire-Risk Prediction

One of the main innovations of FireWatch Cambodia is the integration of machine learning into the harmonized satellite data workflow. Instead of only displaying historical fire observations, we developed and deployed a machine learning model to estimate potential future fire-risk areas across Cambodia.

We implemented and compared three machine learning algorithms: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and Histogram-Based Gradient Boosting. Based on validation performance, the Random Forest Classifier was selected as the final model because it achieved the highest Precision-Recall Area Under the Curve (PR-AUC) among the tested algorithms using the harmonized dataset.

The model uses historical fire-related features derived from the harmonized MODIS and VIIRS hotspot records. These include fire counts over the previous 3, 7, and 30 days, total and mean Fire Radiative Power (FRP) over the previous 7 days, nearby fire counts within neighboring grid cells, the number of days since the last detected fire, and temporal features such as the month and day of the year. For spatial analysis, Cambodia is divided into grid cells measuring 0.1° in both latitude and longitude, equivalent to approximately 11 km.

The model predicts the probability of at least one satellite-detected hotspot occurring in each grid cell within the following three days. The predicted probabilities are then converted into three fire-risk categories: Low, Medium, and High Risk. The classification threshold for Medium Risk is approximately 0.321, selected using the validation dataset, while High Risk is assigned to areas with predicted probabilities of 0.50 or higher. These prediction results are exported as GeoJSON grid polygons and integrated into the FireWatch Cambodia platform, allowing users to explore potential fire-risk areas alongside historical satellite observations.

To evaluate the model's predictive performance, we applied a time-based data split, using observations from 2020 to 2023 for training, 2024 for validation and model selection, and 2025 for independent testing. The final Random Forest model trained on the harmonized dataset achieved a Precision of 62.24%, Recall of 73.92%, F1-Score of 67.58%, PR-AUC of 0.7410, ROC-AUC of 0.9421, and Brier Score of 0.0571 on the 2025 test set. The results also showed improvements in PR-AUC and F1-Score compared with the corresponding MODIS-only and VIIRS-only Random Forest experiments, demonstrating the potential benefits of combining observations from both satellite sensors.

The predictions represent estimated probabilities of future satellite-detected hotspots rather than guaranteed fire occurrences.

2.5. Interactive Web Application

FireWatch Cambodia presents the processed data and analytical results through an interactive web application.

Its main features include:

  • Interactive geographic visualization of fire hotspots.
  • Display of MODIS and VIIRS observations.
  • Visualization of harmonized fire data.
  • Historical fire activity analysis.
  • Machine learning-based future fire-risk predictions.

The application connects data processing, analysis, and prediction in one platform, making satellite-derived information easier to explore and understand.

Users can examine historical hotspot distributions and view predicted risk categories on a geographic map. This helps make complex satellite observations and analytical outputs more accessible to people who may not have technical experience in satellite data processing.

3. Benefits and Intended Impact

FireWatch Cambodia aims to provide several benefits:

Improved Satellite Data Integration: Harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS observations helps address differences between the two datasets and supports more consistent fire monitoring. Instead of examining each satellite source separately, users can explore information from both systems through a unified platform.

Better Understanding of Fire Patterns: Historical analysis helps users explore where and when fire activity occurs across Cambodia. Geographic and seasonal analysis can reveal recurring patterns and changes in hotspot activity over time.

Forward-Looking Risk Assessment: Machine learning predictions extend the platform beyond historical monitoring by identifying areas with potentially higher future fire risk. This provides an additional perspective for understanding possible future hotspot activity.

Accessible Data Visualization: The interactive map makes complex satellite observations and analytical results easier to interpret. Bringing historical observations and predicted risk areas together helps users explore fire-related information in one place.

Environmental Awareness and Decision Support: The platform aims to provide useful information for researchers, environmental organizations, communities, and decision-makers working on fire monitoring and environmental protection.

Long-Term Intended Impact: Our long-term goal is to support more informed fire prevention and preparedness in Cambodia. We hope that the information provided by FireWatch Cambodia can help relevant stakeholders understand fire patterns, identify areas that may require closer attention, and support future environmental protection efforts.

4. Data Science Results and Evaluation

Our data science workflow produces several analytical outputs:

  1. Separate processed MODIS and VIIRS datasets.
  2. Pairwise comparison and matching results between satellite observations.
  3. A harmonized master dataset.
  4. Historical geographic and temporal fire activity analysis.
  5. Machine learning-based future fire-risk predictions.

These outputs were used to analyze historical fire activity across different geographic areas and time periods, as well as to develop a machine learning model for predicting potential future fire-risk areas.

The results were evaluated from two aspects: data harmonization and machine learning performance. The harmonization process was assessed by examining the consistency of satellite observations, the geographic matching between MODIS and VIIRS hotspots, and the differences in their fire detection characteristics.

For machine learning, the selected Random Forest model was evaluated using an independent test dataset from 2025. The evaluation metrics included Precision (62.24%), Recall (73.92%), F1-score (67.58%), PR-AUC (0.7410), ROC-AUC (0.9421), and Brier Score (0.0571).

These metrics provide an assessment of the model's ability to identify potential fire-risk areas and distinguish between grid cells with and without future hotspot activity. The comparison with MODIS-only and VIIRS-only experiments also helps demonstrate the potential value of combining observations from both satellite sensors.

5. Tools and Technologies

The project combines data science, satellite data processing, geospatial analysis, machine learning, and web development.

Area Tools and Technologies

Satellite data NASA FIRMS, MODIS, VIIRS

Data processing Python, Pandas, NumPy

Geospatial analysis GeoPandas,

Data visualization Matplotlib, Plotly

Machine learning Logistic Regression, Random Forest, HistGradientBoosting

Frontend React, Vite, TypeScript

Backend Python, FastAPI

Database PostgreSQL

Deployment Vercel (frontend), Render (backend and database)

Development Environment and Hardware: The project was developed using standard computer equipment and software development environments. Cloud-based deployment services were used to make the web application accessible online. No specialized satellite hardware was required because the project uses publicly available satellite observations provided through NASA FIRMS.

6. Creativity and Innovation

The creativity of FireWatch Cambodia lies in connecting two different NASA satellite observation systems with historical data analysis and machine learning in a single platform.

Rather than treating MODIS and VIIRS as separate sources or simply displaying historical hotspots, our project develops a workflow that harmonizes their observations and uses the resulting data to support future fire-risk prediction.

Another important aspect is the integration of machine learning predictions directly into an interactive geographic platform. Users can explore both historical hotspot observations and predicted future risk areas, making the results more understandable and useful for environmental monitoring.

This combination of satellite data harmonization, data science, machine learning, and interactive visualization creates a more comprehensive approach to understanding fire activity in Cambodia.

7. Limitations and Future Development

Although FireWatch Cambodia provides historical fire monitoring and machine learning-based risk predictions, several improvements can strengthen the platform in the future.

Potential developments include:

  • Improving model performance through additional historical and environmental variables.
  • Conducting further validation using independent fire observations.
  • Improving spatial and temporal prediction resolution.
  • Integrating additional environmental data, such as rainfall, temperature, vegetation, and land-cover information.
  • Connect with real time dataset of the fire from NASA
  • Developing an operational alert mechanism for relevant communities and authorities.

These improvements could help transform FireWatch Cambodia into a more comprehensive fire-risk monitoring and decision-support system.

8. Conclusion

FireWatch Cambodia demonstrates how NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellite observations can be harmonized and enhanced through data science and machine learning. By integrating historical fire analysis, future fire-risk prediction, and interactive visualization, the project goes beyond simply showing where fires have been detected in the past.

Through its interactive platform, users can explore satellite observations, understand historical fire patterns, and examine areas with potentially higher future fire risk. The project brings together satellite data processing, geospatial analysis, machine learning, and web development to make complex fire-related information more accessible.

Ultimately, FireWatch Cambodia aims to make satellite-derived fire information more accessible and useful, contributing to improved environmental monitoring and a better understanding of potential fire risks across Cambodia. We hope this project can provide a foundation for future fire-risk assessment, environmental awareness, and more informed decision-making.
